records.title: Roundtable Meeting Highlights Policy Research on Sand Mining in the Mekong River
records.location: Vientiane Capital, Lao PDR (meeting); sand mining along the Mekong River and its tributaries in Lao PDR
records.summary: On 2 February 2026 in Vientiane, partners in the WWF-Laos and Lao Academy of Social and Economic Sciences project "Safeguarding the Mekong: Advancing Sand Governance and Biodiversity Protection for Climate Resilience in Laos" held a roundtable to present initial research findings on sand mining policies and practices along the Mekong River and its tributaries in Lao PDR. The project is supported by the CARA initiative with UK FCDO funding. According to the article, initial findings and rapid assessments highlighted growing environmental pressures, including riverbank erosion, habitat degradation, biodiversity impacts and potential risks to community livelihoods. Desk reviews identified policy and regulatory gaps, particularly in implementation, coordination and enforcement. Next steps include continued research, awareness-raising, national dialogues, policy briefs and regional knowledge-sharing workshops.
records.limitations: Press release from a project partner; gives no quantitative data, specific river sites or detailed findings; the findings are described as initial. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

records.title: From Tibet to the 'Nine Dragons', Vietnam's Mekong Delta Is Losing Sand
records.dateKind: Publication date stated in article body
records.location: Mo Cay and Ben Tre province, Mekong Delta, Vietnam; Reuters visited three provinces straddling different branches of the delta
records.summary: Reuters reports that upstream damming and extensive riverbed sand mining are causing the land in the Mekong Delta to sink at around 2 cm (0.75 inches) a year, according to experts and officials. Riverbank erosion in Ben Tre province has destroyed homes, such as that of shopkeeper Ta Thi Kim Anh. Can Tho University expert Duong Van Ni says the problem is a lack of sediment and that since China built hydropower plants new sand almost never reaches the delta. The article says sand mining in Cambodia boomed over the last 10 years, partly driven by Singapore demand, and Cambodia banned all sand exports in 2017 under pressure from environmental groups. In Ben Tre, officials describe night-time illegal miners, and a local patrol group claims it got rid of 90 percent of thieves in the first few months, with none approaching since 2018. China's Foreign Ministry and Singapore's Ministry of National Development gave statements on downstream concerns and import controls respectively.
records.limitations: News report relying on attributed statements from officials, experts and locals; no quantified sand extraction volumes; subsidence cause attribution is general (dams and mining) and the 90 percent figure is a patrol member's claim. Automated English summary; native-language review may be needed.

Relevance is plausible: the article covers sand export from the Mekong Delta (ĐBSCL) and sand bought from Cambodia, with expert views on delta erosion and dams on the Mekong. The date is supported by the body quote '04/03/2017 09:41 GMT+7' and the publisher metadata. However, the draft's summary says the 23.7 million m3 for 2007-2009 was 'mainly river sand from the Mekong Delta and sand bought from Cambodia'. The article does support that wording, but the draft's 'countries' list includes Lao PDR, which rests only on a forecast about future dams and not on any extraction or supply chain there. The draft also frames the 11 dams as 'planned' in its location field, while the article only says 'sắp tới' with a forecast. Several expert claims, including the 50 m/year erosion and the 5 km2 loss, are partly about the sea coast and the Red River delta context.
